landmarks.name: BM25
landmarks.maturityNote: Decades of deployment; default lexical scorer in search engines.
landmarks.desc: Probabilistic ranking function scoring documents by term frequency and inverse document frequency; the standard lexical search baseline.

ref.title: Okapi at TREC-3 (Robertson et al.)

landmarks.name: Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search
landmarks.maturityNote: Standard infrastructure in every vector store.
landmarks.desc: Index structures that find near neighbors in high-dimensional vector spaces quickly at slight accuracy cost; the engine inside vector databases.

ref.title: Efficient and robust approximate nearest neighbor search using Hierarchical Navigable Small World graphs (Malkov & Yashunin)

landmarks.name: Open-Domain Question Answering
landmarks.maturityNote: Mature research paradigm, largely absorbed into RAG.
landmarks.desc: Answering questions by retrieving passages from a large corpus and reading them with a neural model; the direct architectural ancestor of RAG.

ref.title: Reading Wikipedia to Answer Open-Domain Questions (Chen et al.)

parents.why: Early systems used lexical retrieval to select passages for a neural reader.

landmarks.name: Attention Mechanism
landmarks.maturityNote: Prerequisite for the transformer.
landmarks.desc: Lets a network weight different parts of its input dynamically when producing each output.

ref.title: Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate (Bahdanau et al.)

landmarks.name: Sequence-to-Sequence Learning
landmarks.maturityNote: Foundational framing for translation and generation.
landmarks.desc: Training networks to map an input sequence to an output sequence end to end.

ref.title: Sequence to Sequence Learning with Neural Networks (Sutskever et al.)

landmarks.name: Transformer
landmarks.maturityNote: Universal architecture for foundation models.
landmarks.desc: Architecture built entirely on self-attention, dispensing with recurrence; the basis of all modern LLMs.

ref.title: Attention Is All You Need (Vaswani et al.)

parents.why: Uses self-attention as the sole sequence-mixing operation.
Replaces recurrent encoder-decoders for sequence transduction.

landmarks.name: Pretrained Language Models
landmarks.maturityNote: The substrate of applied AI engineering.
landmarks.desc: Transformers pretrained on large text corpora with a language-modeling objective, then used directly or adapted; the base every applied technique builds on.

ref.title: Improving Language Understanding by Generative Pre-Training (Radford et al.)

parents.why: Applies the transformer to large-scale unsupervised language modeling.

landmarks.name: Transfer Learning and Fine-Tuning
landmarks.maturityNote: Standard practice across deep learning.
landmarks.desc: Adapting a model pretrained on one task or corpus to a new task by continuing training on targeted data.

ref.title: Universal Language Model Fine-tuning for Text Classification (Howard & Ruder)

landmarks.name: Knowledge Distillation
landmarks.maturityNote: Long-established compression technique.
landmarks.desc: Training a smaller student model to match the outputs of a larger teacher.

ref.title: Distilling the Knowledge in a Neural Network (Hinton et al.)

landmarks.name: Mixture of Experts
landmarks.maturityNote: Standard approach for frontier and large open models; has serving implications.
landmarks.desc: Replaces dense layers with many expert subnetworks and a router that activates a few per token, scaling parameters without proportional compute.

ref.title: Outrageously Large Neural Networks: The Sparsely-Gated Mixture-of-Experts Layer (Shazeer et al.)

external.name: adaptive-mixtures-of-local-experts
external.why: Scales the 1991 mixture-of-experts idea with sparse gating inside deep networks.

landmarks.name: State-Space Models
landmarks.maturityNote: Shipping in hybrid models; not yet a default choice.
landmarks.desc: Sequence models derived from control theory with linear-time scaling in sequence length, used alone or in hybrids with attention.

ref.title: Efficiently Modeling Long Sequences with Structured State Spaces (Gu et al.)

external.name: control-theory-state-space
external.why: Turns continuous state-space equations into trainable sequence layers.

landmarks.name: Heuristic Search
landmarks.maturityNote: Textbook foundation of AI planning.
landmarks.desc: Searching a space of states guided by an estimate of distance to the goal.

ref.title: A Formal Basis for the Heuristic Determination of Minimum Cost Paths (Hart, Nilsson & Raphael)

landmarks.name: STRIPS Planning
landmarks.maturityNote: Historical foundation of symbolic planning.
landmarks.desc: Planning with explicit states, goals, and actions defined by preconditions and effects.

ref.title: STRIPS: A New Approach to the Application of Theorem Proving to Problem Solving (Fikes & Nilsson)

parents.why: Plans are found by searching the state space defined by action models.

landmarks.name: PDDL
landmarks.maturityNote: Established standard; the interface for LLM+planner hybrids.
landmarks.desc: Standard language for describing planning domains and problems so general-purpose solvers can find plans.

ref.title: PDDL — The Planning Domain Definition Language (McDermott et al.)

parents.why: Generalizes STRIPS-style action descriptions into a shared standard.

landmarks.name: Expert Systems
landmarks.maturityNote: Historical; ideas persist in routing and tool modules.
landmarks.desc: Systems that encode domain expertise as explicit rules and route problems through them; an ancestor of modular neuro-symbolic architectures.

ref.title: Computer-Based Medical Consultations: MYCIN (Shortliffe)

landmarks.name: Markov Decision Process
landmarks.maturityNote: Theoretical foundation of RL.
landmarks.desc: Formal model of sequential decision making with states, actions, transitions, and rewards.

ref.title: A Markovian Decision Process (Bellman)

landmarks.name: Policy Gradient Methods
landmarks.maturityNote: Mathematical basis of LLM RL fine-tuning.
landmarks.desc: Optimizing a parameterized policy directly by gradient ascent on expected reward.

ref.title: Policy Gradient Methods for Reinforcement Learning with Function Approximation (Sutton et al.)

parents.why: Optimizes policies defined over MDPs.

landmarks.name: Proximal Policy Optimization
landmarks.maturityNote: Default RL optimizer behind classic RLHF.
landmarks.desc: A policy-gradient algorithm that clips updates to stay near the previous policy, giving stable training.

ref.title: Proximal Policy Optimization Algorithms (Schulman et al.)

parents.why: A clipped-objective policy-gradient method.

landmarks.name: Semantic Networks
landmarks.maturityNote: Historical foundation of graph-structured knowledge.
landmarks.desc: Representing concepts as nodes and relations as labeled edges.

ref.title: Semantic Memory (Quillian)

landmarks.name: Knowledge Graphs
landmarks.maturityNote: Established enterprise and web infrastructure.
landmarks.desc: Large graphs of entities and typed relationships used to store and query structured knowledge.

ref.title: Introducing the Knowledge Graph: things, not strings (Singhal, Google)

parents.why: Scales semantic-network ideas to web-scale entity graphs.

landmarks.name: Conversational Agents
landmarks.maturityNote: Long-standing interaction paradigm.
landmarks.desc: Programs that interact with people through natural-language dialogue.

ref.title: ELIZA — A Computer Program for the Study of Natural Language Communication (Weizenbaum)

landmarks.name: Direct Manipulation
landmarks.maturityNote: Foundational UI principle.
landmarks.desc: Interfaces where users act on visible objects with immediate, reversible feedback.

ref.title: Direct Manipulation: A Step Beyond Programming Languages (Shneiderman)

landmarks.name: Mixed-Initiative Interaction
landmarks.maturityNote: Established HCI framework, newly central with LLM assistants.
landmarks.desc: Designing systems where the user and an automated agent each take initiative, with the system weighing when to act, ask, or defer.

ref.title: Principles of Mixed-Initiative User Interfaces (Horvitz, CHI 1999)

parents.why: Unifies direct-manipulation interfaces with automated agents.

landmarks.name: Least Privilege
landmarks.maturityNote: Core security design principle.
landmarks.desc: Every component should operate with only the permissions it needs.

ref.title: The Protection of Information in Computer Systems (Saltzer & Schroeder)

landmarks.name: Sandboxing and Isolation
landmarks.maturityNote: Essential infrastructure.
landmarks.desc: Running untrusted code in restricted environments that cannot affect the host.

ref.title: A Secure Environment for Untrusted Helper Applications (Goldberg et al., USENIX Security 1996)

parents.why: Enforces minimal authority on untrusted code.

landmarks.name: Injection Attacks
landmarks.maturityNote: Classic, well-understood vulnerability class.
landmarks.desc: Attacks where untrusted data is interpreted as instructions because data and control share a channel.

ref.title: NT Web Technology Vulnerabilities (rain.forest.puppy, Phrack 54) — early public SQL injection write-up

landmarks.name: Statecharts and State Machines
landmarks.maturityNote: Standard modeling technique.
landmarks.desc: Modeling system behavior as explicit states and transitions, including hierarchy and concurrency.

ref.title: Statecharts: A Visual Formalism for Complex Systems (Harel)

landmarks.name: Test-Driven Development
landmarks.maturityNote: Established engineering practice.
landmarks.desc: Writing tests that define expected behavior before or alongside the code, and gating changes on them.

ref.title: Test-Driven Development: By Example (Beck)

landmarks.name: Distributed Tracing
landmarks.maturityNote: Standard observability infrastructure.
landmarks.desc: Recording the causal tree of operations across services so latency and failures can be attributed.

ref.title: Dapper, a Large-Scale Distributed Systems Tracing Infrastructure (Sigelman et al., Google)

landmarks.name: Language Server Protocol
landmarks.maturityNote: Ubiquitous editor standard; explicit inspiration for MCP.
landmarks.desc: A JSON-RPC protocol that decouples editors from language tooling, solving an N×M integration problem.

ref.title: Language Server Protocol (Microsoft)

landmarks.name: Autoregressive Decoding
landmarks.maturityNote: The baseline execution pattern of every generative model.
landmarks.desc: Generating text one token at a time, each conditioned on everything generated so far, using a sampling strategy.

ref.title: Improving Language Understanding by Generative Pre-Training (Radford et al.)

parents.why: The generation loop for causal language models.

landmarks.name: KV Cache
landmarks.maturityNote: Non-negotiable serving infrastructure.
landmarks.desc: Storing attention keys and values from earlier tokens so each decoding step avoids recomputation; its memory footprint dominates serving design.

ref.title: Fast Transformer Decoding: One Write-Head is All You Need (Shazeer)

parents.why: Memoizes attention state across decoding steps.

landmarks.name: PagedAttention
landmarks.maturityNote: Dominant memory-management approach in serving engines.
landmarks.desc: Stores the KV cache in non-contiguous fixed-size blocks, like OS virtual memory, cutting fragmentation and raising batch sizes.

ref.title: Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention (Kwon et al.)

parents.why: Applies virtual-memory paging to KV cache storage.

landmarks.name: Continuous Batching
landmarks.maturityNote: Required for production-scale serving.
landmarks.desc: Scheduling at the level of decoding steps so new requests join and finished ones leave a batch continuously.

ref.title: Orca: A Distributed Serving System for Transformer-Based Generative Models (Yu et al., OSDI 2022)

parents.why: Schedules per decoding iteration rather than per request.

landmarks.name: Speculative Decoding
landmarks.maturityNote: Broadly integrated into serving engines; variants (Medusa, EAGLE) still evolving.
landmarks.desc: A small draft model or head proposes several tokens that the target model verifies in parallel, reducing latency without changing outputs.

ref.title: Fast Inference from Transformers via Speculative Decoding (Leviathan et al.)

parents.why: Breaks the strictly serial decode loop with parallel verification.

landmarks.name: Weight Quantization
landmarks.maturityNote: Standard for local and cost-sensitive serving.
landmarks.desc: Storing weights at lower numerical precision to cut memory and bandwidth with minimal quality loss.

ref.title: LLM.int8(): 8-bit Matrix Multiplication for Transformers at Scale (Dettmers et al.)

parents.why: Applies low-precision numerics to transformer weight matrices.

landmarks.name: KV Cache Quantization
landmarks.maturityNote: Supported in major engines; methods still competing.
landmarks.desc: Storing cached keys and values at reduced precision to fit longer contexts and larger batches in memory.

ref.title: KIVI: A Tuning-Free Asymmetric 2bit Quantization for KV Cache (Liu et al.)

parents.why: Targets the KV cache's memory footprint specifically.
Applies quantization to activation state rather than weights.

landmarks.name: Prompt Caching
landmarks.maturityNote: Offered by major API providers; shapes how prompts are structured.
landmarks.desc: Reusing the computed KV cache for shared prompt prefixes across requests, cutting prefill cost and latency.

ref.title: SGLang: Efficient Execution of Structured Language Model Programs (Zheng et al.)

parents.why: Turns the KV cache into a long-lived, shared asset across requests.

landmarks.name: Constrained Decoding
landmarks.maturityNote: Backs the structured-output features of major APIs.
landmarks.desc: Masking invalid tokens at each decoding step so output is guaranteed to match a grammar or schema.

ref.title: Synchromesh: Reliable Code Generation from Pre-trained Language Models (Poesia et al.)

parents.why: Restricts the sampling step to tokens valid under a grammar.

landmarks.name: Model Routing and Cascades
landmarks.maturityNote: In production at cost-sensitive companies; techniques still unsettled.
landmarks.desc: Sending each request to the cheapest model likely to handle it well, or escalating through a cascade of models.

ref.title: FrugalGPT: How to Use Large Language Models While Reducing Cost and Improving Performance (Chen et al.)

parents.why: Lifts learned routing from experts within a model to whole models.

landmarks.name: Prefill-Decode Disaggregation
landmarks.maturityNote: Adopted by large-scale providers; becoming standard in open engines.
landmarks.desc: Running the compute-bound prefill phase and the memory-bound decode phase on separate hardware pools, transferring KV state between them.

ref.title: DistServe: Disaggregating Prefill and Decoding for Goodput-optimized LLM Serving (Zhong et al.)

parents.why: Separates the two phases continuous batching interleaves on one device.
Requires moving KV cache between prefill and decode workers.

landmarks.name: Local and On-Device Inference
landmarks.maturityNote: Mature tooling and a large user base.
landmarks.desc: Running models on consumer hardware or devices, relying on quantization and efficient kernels.

ref.title: llama.cpp (Gerganov)

parents.why: Quantization makes models fit consumer memory.

landmarks.name: Zero-Shot Prompting
landmarks.maturityNote: Baseline interaction mode for instruction-tuned models.
landmarks.desc: Asking a model to perform a task from instructions alone, with no examples.

ref.title: Language Models are Unsupervised Multitask Learners (Radford et al.)

parents.why: Uses a pretrained model's latent task knowledge directly.

landmarks.name: Few-Shot Prompting
landmarks.maturityNote: Standard steering technique.
landmarks.desc: Including example input-output pairs in the prompt to condition format and behavior.

ref.title: Language Models are Few-Shot Learners (Brown et al.)

parents.why: Adds demonstrations to instructions.

landmarks.name: System Prompts
landmarks.maturityNote: Built into every major chat API.
landmarks.desc: A privileged, persistent instruction block that defines role, constraints, and behavior for a conversation.

ref.title: Introducing ChatGPT and Whisper APIs (OpenAI, March 2023)

parents.why: A persistent, privileged form of instruction.

landmarks.name: Prompt Templating
landmarks.maturityNote: Ubiquitous in LLM applications.
landmarks.desc: Separating fixed prompt structure from variable data using templating, so prompts can be versioned and reused.

ref.title: LangChain initial release (Chase, October 2022)

parents.why: Turns hand-written prompts into reusable software artifacts.

external.name: template-engines
external.why: Reuses standard text templating from web development.

landmarks.name: Prompt Chaining
landmarks.maturityNote: Foundational pattern behind most LLM workflows.
landmarks.desc: Decomposing a task into a fixed sequence of LLM calls, each consuming the previous call's output.

ref.title: AI Chains: Transparent and Controllable Human-AI Interaction by Chaining Large Language Model Prompts (Wu et al.)

parents.why: Composes multiple prompts into a pipeline.
Originated as an HCI technique for transparent, controllable human-AI collaboration.

landmarks.name: Structured Outputs
landmarks.maturityNote: Standard for connecting models to code.
landmarks.desc: Getting models to emit machine-readable data matching a schema, through prompting, validation, or constrained decoding.

ref.title: Efficient Guided Generation for Large Language Models (Willard & Louf)

parents.why: Demonstrations of the target format were the original technique.
Grammar-constrained decoding makes schema adherence guaranteed.

landmarks.name: Context Compaction
landmarks.maturityNote: Common in agent harnesses; techniques still forming.
landmarks.desc: Compressing, summarizing, or pruning context so long tasks fit within the window without losing what matters.

ref.title: LLMLingua: Compressing Prompts for Accelerated Inference of Large Language Models (Jiang et al.)

parents.why: Uses language models to compress text for other model calls.

landmarks.name: Context Engineering
landmarks.maturityNote: Widely adopted term and practice; best practices still forming.
landmarks.desc: Curating the entire set of tokens a model sees — instructions, tools, retrieved data, history, memory — as a finite resource, especially for long-running agents.

ref.title: Effective context engineering for AI agents (Anthropic)

parents.why: Generalizes prompt writing to managing all context state.
Compaction is one of its core long-horizon techniques.
Just-in-time retrieval of context is part of the discipline.

landmarks.name: Automatic Prompt Optimization
landmarks.maturityNote: Moving into production pipelines.
landmarks.desc: Using models and search to generate, score, and refine prompts against a dataset instead of tuning them by hand.

ref.title: Large Language Models Are Human-Level Prompt Engineers (Zhou et al.)

parents.why: Uses LLM generation to propose instructions.

landmarks.name: Declarative Prompt Compilation
landmarks.maturityNote: Real adoption; still a minority approach.
landmarks.desc: Writing LM pipelines as declarative modules with signatures, then compiling prompts and few-shot examples automatically with optimizers.

ref.title: DSPy: Compiling Declarative Language Model Calls into Self-Improving Pipelines (Khattab et al.)

parents.why: Turns prompt optimization into a programming model.
Optimizes multi-stage pipelines rather than single prompts.

landmarks.name: Text Embeddings
landmarks.maturityNote: Bedrock of semantic search.
landmarks.desc: Models that map text to vectors so that semantically similar texts are close together.

ref.title: Sentence-BERT: Sentence Embeddings using Siamese BERT-Networks (Reimers & Gurevych)

parents.why: Fine-tunes pretrained encoders to produce comparable sentence vectors.

landmarks.name: Dense Retrieval
landmarks.maturityNote: Standard mechanism of vector databases.
landmarks.desc: Retrieving documents by embedding queries and passages into a shared vector space and searching by similarity.

ref.title: Dense Passage Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering (Karpukhin et al.)

parents.why: Uses learned embeddings as the retrieval representation.
Depends on ANN indexes to search at scale.
Positioned as a learned replacement for sparse retrieval.

landmarks.name: Retrieval-Augmented Generation
landmarks.maturityNote: The default pattern for grounding applications.
landmarks.desc: Retrieving relevant passages and placing them in the model's context so generation is grounded in external knowledge.

ref.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks (Lewis et al.)

parents.why: Replaces the extractive reader with a generative model.
Uses dense retrieval as the retriever.
Uses a pretrained generator.

landmarks.name: Chunking Strategies
landmarks.maturityNote: Well understood; variants still evolving.
landmarks.desc: Splitting documents into passages sized and bounded for embedding and retrieval.

ref.title: LangChain text splitters documentation

parents.why: Required preprocessing for passage-level retrieval.

landmarks.name: Hybrid Search
landmarks.maturityNote: Recommended production baseline.
landmarks.desc: Combining lexical and vector retrieval, typically fusing rankings, to catch both exact terms and semantic matches.

ref.title: Reciprocal Rank Fusion Outperforms Condorcet and Individual Rank Learning Methods (Cormack et al., SIGIR 2009)

parents.why: Contributes exact-term matching.
Contributes semantic matching.

landmarks.name: Cross-Encoder Reranking
landmarks.maturityNote: Standard in high-accuracy retrieval.
landmarks.desc: Rescoring a candidate set by passing query and document jointly through a transformer for a precise relevance score.

ref.title: Passage Re-ranking with BERT (Nogueira & Cho)

parents.why: Uses a pretrained transformer as a relevance scorer.
Introduced as a second stage over first-stage lexical retrieval.

landmarks.name: Query Rewriting and HyDE
landmarks.maturityNote: Common in advanced pipelines; adds latency.
landmarks.desc: Using a model to rewrite, expand, or answer hypothetically before retrieval, improving recall for short or vague queries.

ref.title: Precise Zero-Shot Dense Retrieval without Relevance Labels (Gao et al.)

parents.why: Changes the query representation fed to the retriever.

landmarks.name: Contextual Retrieval
landmarks.maturityNote: Widely copied pattern; relies on prompt caching for cost.
landmarks.desc: Prepending model-generated document context to each chunk before embedding and indexing, reducing retrieval failures from orphaned chunks.

ref.title: Introducing Contextual Retrieval (Anthropic)

parents.why: Restores document context lost by chunking.
Applied to both embedding and BM25 indexes.

landmarks.name: GraphRAG
landmarks.maturityNote: High interest; indexing cost limits production use.
landmarks.desc: Using models to extract an entity graph from a corpus, cluster it into communities, and summarize them to answer global questions.

ref.title: From Local to Global: A Graph RAG Approach to Query-Focused Summarization (Edge et al.)

parents.why: Keeps retrieval-then-generate structure.
Builds and traverses a knowledge graph automatically.

landmarks.name: Self-RAG
landmarks.maturityNote: Influential research; patterns absorbed into agentic RAG.
landmarks.desc: Training a model to decide when to retrieve and to critique its own generations with reflection tokens.

ref.title: Self-RAG: Learning to Retrieve, Generate, and Critique through Self-Reflection (Asai et al.)

parents.why: Makes retrieval adaptive and self-critiqued.

landmarks.name: Corrective RAG
landmarks.maturityNote: Common in templates; limited evidence of broad production use.
landmarks.desc: Grading retrieved documents and falling back to web search or refinement when retrieval quality is low.

ref.title: Corrective Retrieval Augmented Generation (Yan et al.)

parents.why: Adds a retrieval evaluator and corrective actions.

landmarks.name: Agentic RAG
landmarks.maturityNote: In enterprise production; agentic search increasingly replaces fixed pipelines.
landmarks.desc: Letting an agent plan queries, choose sources and tools, and iterate retrieval until it has enough to answer.
examples: agentic file search in coding agents

ref.title: Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation: A Survey on Agentic RAG (Singh et al.)

parents.why: Retrieval remains the core goal.
Wraps retrieval in an agent loop.
Generalizes adaptive, self-critiqued retrieval.

landmarks.name: MRKL Systems
landmarks.maturityNote: Concept absorbed into standard tool use.
landmarks.desc: Architectures that route parts of a query from an LLM to discrete expert modules such as calculators, APIs, and databases.

ref.title: MRKL Systems: A modular, neuro-symbolic architecture that combines large language models, external knowledge sources and discrete reasoning (Karpas et al.)

parents.why: Revives modular expert routing with an LLM as the router.
The language model handles understanding and routing.

landmarks.name: Tool Learning
landmarks.maturityNote: Tool use is now trained into every frontier model.
landmarks.desc: Training models to decide when and how to call tools by inserting API calls into their own training data.
examples: tool-use training data in frontier models

ref.title: Toolformer: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Use Tools (Schick et al.)

parents.why: Learns tool invocation rather than hand-routing.
Uses few-shot prompting to annotate candidate API calls.

landmarks.name: Function Calling
landmarks.maturityNote: Core primitive of every major model API.
landmarks.desc: A model emits a structured call matching a declared schema; the host executes it and returns the result to the model.

ref.title: Function calling and other API updates (OpenAI, June 2023)

parents.why: Productizes trained tool use as an API contract.
Calls are schema-conformant structured output.

landmarks.name: ReAct Agent Loop
landmarks.maturityNote: The canonical agent loop.
landmarks.desc: Interleaving reasoning traces with actions and observations in a loop until the task is done.

ref.title: ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models (Yao et al.)

parents.why: Supplies the reasoning half of the loop.
Supplies the acting half via external tools.

landmarks.name: Workflow Graphs and State Machines
landmarks.maturityNote: Preferred production pattern for reliable agentic applications.
landmarks.desc: Orchestrating LLM calls as explicit graphs of states and transitions in code, with the model deciding only where it must.

ref.title: Building effective agents (Anthropic, December 2024)

parents.why: Applies state-machine modeling to LLM control flow.
Adds branching, cycles, and persistent state to fixed chains.
Replaces model-driven control flow where reliability matters.

landmarks.name: Model Context Protocol
landmarks.maturityNote: Adopted across major clients and providers within a year of launch.
landmarks.desc: An open JSON-RPC protocol for connecting AI applications to tools, data, and prompts through interchangeable servers.

ref.title: Model Context Protocol specification

parents.why: Standardizes how tools are described and invoked across hosts.
Explicitly modeled on LSP's approach to the N×M integration problem.

landmarks.name: Agent Memory
landmarks.maturityNote: Shipping in assistants; designs vary widely.
landmarks.desc: Persisting information across turns and sessions — transcripts, extracted facts, notes — and bringing it back into context when relevant.

ref.title: MemGPT: Towards LLMs as Operating Systems (Packer et al.)

parents.why: Applies retrieval to an agent's own history.
Pages information in and out of the window.

landmarks.name: Multi-Agent Systems
landmarks.maturityNote: Orchestrator-subagent patterns in production; free-form swarms still unreliable.
landmarks.desc: Several agents with distinct roles or contexts that delegate, collaborate, or debate to complete a task.

ref.title: AutoGen: Enabling Next-Gen LLM Applications via Multi-Agent Conversation (Wu et al.)

parents.why: Composes multiple agent loops with message passing.

external.name: classical-multi-agent-systems
external.why: Revives distributed AI ideas with LLM agents.

landmarks.name: Coding Agents
landmarks.maturityNote: Mainstream developer tooling by 2025–2026.
landmarks.desc: Agents with shell, file system, and test access that make and verify changes to codebases.

ref.title: SWE-agent: Agent-Computer Interfaces Enable Automated Software Engineering (Yang et al.)

parents.why: An agent loop specialized to software environments.
Acts through tools for editing, searching, and running code.

landmarks.name: Computer-Use Agents
landmarks.maturityNote: Shipping in products; reliability still limits unattended use.
landmarks.desc: Agents that perceive screens and operate graphical interfaces with mouse and keyboard actions.

ref.title: Introducing computer use (Anthropic, October 2024)

parents.why: An agent loop whose environment is a GUI.
Requires visual understanding of screens.

landmarks.name: Deep Research Agents
landmarks.maturityNote: Shipping in all major assistants; quality varies.
landmarks.desc: Long-running agents that plan, search many sources, read, and synthesize a cited report.

ref.title: How we built our multi-agent research system (Anthropic)

parents.why: Scales iterative retrieval to open-ended, multi-source research.
Often implemented with orchestrator and parallel subagents.

landmarks.name: Agent Skills
landmarks.maturityNote: Recently introduced; adoption spreading across agent platforms.
landmarks.desc: Packaging instructions, scripts, and resources as folders an agent loads on demand, disclosing detail progressively to save context.

ref.title: Equipping agents for the real world with Agent Skills (Anthropic)

parents.why: Progressive disclosure keeps context lean.
Complements tool protocols with procedural knowledge.

landmarks.name: Scratchpads
landmarks.maturityNote: Idea fully absorbed into chain-of-thought.
landmarks.desc: Training or prompting models to write intermediate computation steps before the final answer.

ref.title: Show Your Work: Scratchpads for Intermediate Computation with Language Models (Nye et al.)

parents.why: Has the model emit intermediate steps as text.

landmarks.name: Chain-of-Thought
landmarks.maturityNote: Built into modern models and reasoning systems.
landmarks.desc: Eliciting intermediate reasoning steps before a final answer, improving performance on multi-step problems.

ref.title: Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models (Wei et al.)

parents.why: Adds rationales to few-shot demonstrations.
Generalizes scratchpads via prompting alone (contested lineage).

landmarks.name: Self-Consistency
landmarks.maturityNote: Standard accuracy technique.
landmarks.desc: Sampling several reasoning paths and taking the most common answer.

ref.title: Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning in Language Models (Wang et al.)

parents.why: Aggregates multiple CoT samples.

landmarks.name: Tree Search over Reasoning
landmarks.maturityNote: Expensive; mostly research and high-value async tasks.
landmarks.desc: Exploring a tree of partial reasoning states with evaluation, lookahead, and backtracking.

ref.title: Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models (Yao et al.)

parents.why: Expands a single chain into a searched tree.
Brings classical search (BFS/DFS, MCTS) to generated thoughts.

landmarks.name: Self-Reflection
landmarks.maturityNote: Common pattern; gains depend heavily on feedback quality.
landmarks.desc: Having a model critique its own output or trajectory and retry with the critique in context.

ref.title: Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning (Shinn et al.)

parents.why: Adds verbal self-feedback across agent trials.

landmarks.name: Process Reward Models
landmarks.maturityNote: Influential; outcome-based verification has proven easier to scale.
landmarks.desc: Reward models that score each reasoning step rather than only the final answer, used to guide search and training.

ref.title: Let's Verify Step by Step (Lightman et al.)

parents.why: A step-level variant of the learned reward model.

landmarks.name: Test-Time Compute Scaling
landmarks.maturityNote: Reshaped how systems trade latency and cost for quality.
landmarks.desc: Spending more computation at inference — longer reasoning, more samples, search — to improve answers, with predictable returns.

ref.title: Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters (Snell et al.)

parents.why: Formalizes sampling-based gains as a scaling relationship.
Includes search-based allocation strategies.

landmarks.name: Reasoning Models
landmarks.maturityNote: Available from all major providers; standard for hard tasks.
landmarks.desc: Models trained with RL to produce long internal reasoning before answering, with controllable thinking budgets.

ref.title: DeepSeek-R1: Incentivizing Reasoning Capability in LLMs via Reinforcement Learning

parents.why: Internalizes long chains of thought through training.
Turns extra inference compute into a native model capability.
Trained with large-scale RL.

landmarks.name: LLM+P
landmarks.maturityNote: Research prototypes; foundational for neuro-symbolic planning.
landmarks.desc: The LLM translates a natural-language problem into PDDL, a classical planner solves it, and the LLM translates the plan back.

ref.title: LLM+P: Empowering Large Language Models with Optimal Planning Proficiency (Liu et al.)

parents.why: Uses PDDL and an off-the-shelf planner for correctness.
Uses the LLM as translator between language and formal specification.

landmarks.name: LLM-Modulo
landmarks.maturityNote: Prototyped in planning domains; ideas echo in verifier-based agents.
landmarks.desc: LLMs generate candidate plans that a bank of external verifiers and critics checks, iterating until a plan passes.

ref.title: LLMs Can't Plan, But Can Help Planning in LLM-Modulo Frameworks (Kambhampati et al.)

parents.why: Generalizes from translation to generate-and-verify with multiple critics.
Uses LLM reasoning to propose candidates.

landmarks.name: Supervised Fine-Tuning
landmarks.maturityNote: Standard step in every model release.
landmarks.desc: Training a pretrained model on curated instruction-response pairs to follow instructions and adopt a format.

ref.title: Finetuned Language Models Are Zero-Shot Learners (Wei et al.)

parents.why: Fine-tuning on instruction-following data.

landmarks.name: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning
landmarks.maturityNote: Standard for resource-constrained adaptation.
landmarks.desc: Fine-tuning only a small set of added or selected parameters, cutting memory and storage costs.

ref.title: Parameter-Efficient Transfer Learning for NLP (Houlsby et al.)

parents.why: Restricts fine-tuning to a small parameter subset.

landmarks.name: LoRA
landmarks.maturityNote: Default open-source adaptation method.
landmarks.desc: Freezing base weights and training small low-rank update matrices injected into each layer.

ref.title: LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models (Hu et al.)

parents.why: Low-rank decomposition as the parameter-efficient mechanism.

landmarks.name: RLHF
landmarks.maturityNote: Established for frontier alignment; increasingly mixed with other methods.
landmarks.desc: Training a reward model on human preference comparisons, then optimizing the policy against it with RL.

ref.title: Deep Reinforcement Learning from Human Preferences (Christiano et al.); applied to LLMs in InstructGPT (Ouyang et al. 2022)

parents.why: Optimizes a policy against a learned reward.

external.name: preference-learning
external.why: Learns a reward from pairwise human comparisons.

landmarks.name: Direct Preference Optimization
landmarks.maturityNote: Widely used in open-model post-training.
landmarks.desc: Optimizing the model directly on preference pairs with a classification-style loss, removing the separate reward model and RL loop.

ref.title: Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model (Rafailov et al.)

parents.why: Achieves preference alignment without PPO or an explicit reward model.

landmarks.name: Constitutional AI and RLAIF
landmarks.maturityNote: Core to at least one frontier lab; AI feedback widely used.
landmarks.desc: Using a model guided by written principles to critique, revise, and rank outputs, replacing much of the human preference labeling.

ref.title: Constitutional AI: Harmlessness from AI Feedback (Bai et al.)

parents.why: Replaces human preference labels with AI feedback guided by principles.

landmarks.name: RL with Verifiable Rewards
landmarks.maturityNote: Standard ingredient of reasoning-model training since 2025.
landmarks.desc: Keeping the RLHF objective but replacing the learned reward model with a programmatic verifier such as answer checks or unit tests.

ref.title: Tülu 3: Pushing Frontiers in Open Language Model Post-Training (Lambert et al.)

parents.why: Same KL-constrained RL objective with a verifier instead of a reward model.
Tülu 3 optimized RLVR with PPO.

landmarks.name: Group Relative Policy Optimization
landmarks.maturityNote: Algorithm of choice for open reasoning RL after DeepSeek-R1.
landmarks.desc: A policy-gradient method that baselines each response against a group of samples for the same prompt, removing the value network.

ref.title: DeepSeekMath: Pushing the Limits of Mathematical Reasoning in Open Language Models (Shao et al.)

parents.why: PPO-style objective with group-relative advantages instead of a critic.

landmarks.name: LLM Distillation
landmarks.maturityNote: Pervasive for small and open models.
landmarks.desc: Fine-tuning smaller models on outputs and rationales generated by larger ones.

ref.title: Distilling Step-by-Step! Outperforming Larger Language Models with Less Training Data and Smaller Model Sizes (Hsieh et al.)

parents.why: Applies teacher-student training to generated text and rationales.
Implemented as SFT on teacher outputs.

landmarks.name: Self-Instruct
landmarks.maturityNote: Established technique behind many open instruction sets.
landmarks.desc: Bootstrapping instruction datasets by prompting a model to generate tasks, inputs, and outputs from a few seeds.

ref.title: Self-Instruct: Aligning Language Models with Self-Generated Instructions (Wang et al.)

parents.why: Uses few-shot prompts seeded with example tasks to generate new ones.

landmarks.name: Evol-Instruct
landmarks.maturityNote: Influential; one of many synthetic recipes.
landmarks.desc: Iteratively rewriting instructions to be harder or broader, producing more complex training data.

ref.title: WizardLM: Empowering Large Language Models to Follow Complex Instructions (Xu et al.)

parents.why: Evolves generated instructions for difficulty and diversity.

landmarks.name: Synthetic Pretraining Data
landmarks.maturityNote: Common in frontier and small-model training.
landmarks.desc: Generating large, high-quality synthetic corpora with strong models to pretrain or mid-train smaller ones.

ref.title: Textbooks Are All You Need (Gunasekar et al.)

parents.why: Scales model-generated data from instructions to full training corpora.

landmarks.name: Crowdsourced Instruction Data
landmarks.maturityNote: Established, though increasingly supplemented by synthetic data.
landmarks.desc: Collecting instruction and conversation data written and rated by people.

ref.title: OpenAssistant Conversations — Democratizing Large Language Model Alignment (Köpf et al.)

external.name: crowdsourcing
external.why: Applies crowdsourcing to conversational training data.

landmarks.name: LLM-Assisted Annotation
landmarks.maturityNote: Routine in data pipelines.
landmarks.desc: Using models to label or classify data in place of, or alongside, human annotators.

ref.title: ChatGPT Outperforms Crowd-Workers for Text-Annotation Tasks (Gilardi et al.)

parents.why: Annotation as a zero-shot classification task.

landmarks.name: Data Deduplication
landmarks.maturityNote: Standard corpus hygiene.
landmarks.desc: Removing exact and near-duplicate documents from training corpora to improve quality and reduce memorization.

ref.title: Deduplicating Training Data Makes Language Models Better (Lee et al.)

external.name: minhash
external.why: Uses locality-sensitive hashing for near-duplicate detection.

landmarks.name: Data Decontamination
landmarks.maturityNote: Expected in serious releases; imperfectly practiced.
landmarks.desc: Removing training data that overlaps with evaluation benchmarks so scores reflect real capability.

ref.title: Language Models are Few-Shot Learners, contamination analysis (Brown et al.)

external.name: n-gram-overlap-detection
external.why: Detects benchmark overlap by n-gram matching.

landmarks.name: Data Quality Filtering
landmarks.maturityNote: Standard in pretraining pipelines.
landmarks.desc: Selecting high-value training text with heuristics and model-based quality classifiers.

ref.title: The FineWeb Datasets: Decanting the Web for the Finest Text Data at Scale (Penedo et al.)

parents.why: Builds on deduplicated corpora with quality scoring.
Trains quality classifiers on LLM-annotated samples.

landmarks.name: Capability Benchmarks
landmarks.maturityNote: Universal, though saturation and contamination limit value.
landmarks.desc: Fixed datasets with reference answers used to compare model capabilities.

ref.title: Measuring Massive Multitask Language Understanding (Hendrycks et al.)

external.name: shared-task-benchmarks
external.why: Continues NLP's tradition of shared benchmark datasets.

landmarks.name: Long-Context Evals
landmarks.maturityNote: Cited with every long-context release; harder variants replacing NIAH.
landmarks.desc: Tests of whether models retrieve and use information placed at various depths in very long inputs.

ref.title: Needle In A Haystack — Pressure Testing LLMs (Kamradt)

parents.why: Benchmarks targeted at long-context recall and reasoning.

landmarks.name: Agent Benchmarks
landmarks.maturityNote: Central to agent progress reporting; methodology still contested.
landmarks.desc: Evaluating agents by whether they complete tasks in real or simulated environments, judged by tests or state checks.

ref.title: SWE-bench: Can Language Models Resolve Real-World GitHub Issues? (Jimenez et al.)

parents.why: Benchmarks whose items are tasks in environments.
Grades with fail-to-pass and pass-to-pass tests.

landmarks.name: LLM-as-a-Judge
landmarks.maturityNote: Standard for open-ended evaluation; reliability caveats well documented.
landmarks.desc: Using a strong model with a rubric to grade or compare outputs where exact answers don't exist.

ref.title: Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena (Zheng et al.)

parents.why: Grading is posed as an instructed evaluation task.

landmarks.name: Pairwise Preference Evaluation
landmarks.maturityNote: Widely cited; known biases toward style.
landmarks.desc: Comparing two anonymous responses side by side, by humans or judges, and aggregating into ratings.

ref.title: Chatbot Arena: An Open Platform for Evaluating LLMs by Human Preference (Chiang et al.)

external.name: elo-rating
external.why: Aggregates pairwise votes with Elo/Bradley-Terry ratings.

landmarks.name: RAG Evaluation
landmarks.maturityNote: Common practice; metrics still debated.
landmarks.desc: Measuring retrieval quality and grounded answer faithfulness, often with model-graded metrics.

ref.title: RAGAS: Automated Evaluation of Retrieval Augmented Generation (Es et al.)

parents.why: Judges specialized to faithfulness and relevance.
Targets RAG pipeline components.

landmarks.name: Eval-Driven Development
landmarks.maturityNote: Mainstream in mature AI teams; tooling consolidating.
landmarks.desc: Gating prompt, model, and pipeline changes on eval suites run in CI, the way tests gate code.

ref.title: Demystifying evals for AI agents (Anthropic)

parents.why: Carries test-first discipline to stochastic systems.
Uses model graders for open-ended cases.

landmarks.name: LLM Tracing
landmarks.maturityNote: Expected in production systems.
landmarks.desc: Capturing nested spans for model calls, retrieval, and tool use to debug quality, latency, and cost.

ref.title: OpenTelemetry Semantic Conventions for Generative AI

parents.why: Applies span-based tracing to LLM pipelines.

landmarks.name: Online Evaluation and Monitoring
landmarks.maturityNote: Growing practice; methods and tooling still forming.
landmarks.desc: Scoring live traffic with automated graders and user signals to catch regressions and drift after deployment.

ref.title: Langfuse / Arize documentation on online evaluation

parents.why: Runs evaluators over captured production traces.
Uses model graders on sampled traffic.

landmarks.name: Prompt Injection
landmarks.maturityNote: Well-characterized threat; no complete fix.
landmarks.desc: Attacks in which text supplied by a user or third party is followed as instructions, overriding the developer's intent.

ref.title: Ignore Previous Prompt: Attack Techniques For Language Models (Perez & Ribeiro)

parents.why: The classic data-as-instructions flaw, where data and instructions share one channel.
Exploits instruction-following itself.

landmarks.name: Indirect Prompt Injection
landmarks.maturityNote: The central security problem for agents.
landmarks.desc: Injection delivered through retrieved documents, web pages, emails, or tool outputs rather than the user's own message.

ref.title: Not what you've signed up for: Compromising Real-World LLM-Integrated Applications with Indirect Prompt Injection (Greshake et al.)

parents.why: Injection through third-party content.
Exploits content pulled into context.

landmarks.name: Jailbreaks
landmarks.maturityNote: Well-studied attack class; arms race ongoing.
landmarks.desc: Inputs crafted to make a model violate its own safety training.

ref.title: Jailbroken: How Does LLM Safety Training Fail? (Wei et al.)

parents.why: Attacks the behaviors instilled by safety training.

landmarks.name: AI Red Teaming
landmarks.maturityNote: Standard pre-release practice at major labs.
landmarks.desc: Systematic adversarial testing by people and models to find harmful behaviors and vulnerabilities before release.

ref.title: Red Teaming Language Models with Language Models (Perez et al.)

parents.why: Probes for failures of safety-trained behavior.

external.name: security-red-teaming
external.why: Adapts adversarial testing from security practice.

landmarks.name: Guardrails and Safety Classifiers
landmarks.maturityNote: Widely deployed in enterprise stacks.
landmarks.desc: Classifiers and rule layers that check inputs and outputs for policy violations, PII, or unsafe content.

ref.title: Llama Guard: LLM-based Input-Output Safeguard for Human-AI Conversations (Inan et al.)

parents.why: Many guards are LLMs prompted or fine-tuned as classifiers.

external.name: content-moderation-classifiers
external.why: Extends content moderation to model inputs and outputs.

landmarks.name: Prompt Injection Defenses
landmarks.maturityNote: Deployed in frontier models; known to be incomplete.
landmarks.desc: Training, prompting, and architectural measures that make models distinguish trusted instructions from untrusted data.

ref.title: The Instruction Hierarchy: Training LLMs to Prioritize Privileged Instructions (Wallace et al.)

parents.why: Mitigates injection.
Mitigates injection via third-party content.

landmarks.name: Agent Sandboxing and Permissions
landmarks.maturityNote: Standard for any agent that executes code.
landmarks.desc: Running agent actions in isolated environments with scoped credentials and explicit permission prompts to limit damage.

ref.title: E2B — open-source cloud sandboxes for AI agents

parents.why: Applies isolation to LLM-generated code and actions.
Scopes tools and credentials to what a task needs.
Contains the risks of models triggering real actions and code execution.

landmarks.name: Mechanistic Interpretability
landmarks.maturityNote: Primarily research; early engineering uses emerging.
landmarks.desc: Reverse-engineering the internal mechanisms of neural networks into human-understandable features and circuits.

ref.title: A Mathematical Framework for Transformer Circuits (Elhage et al.)

parents.why: Studies transformer internals directly.

landmarks.name: Sparse Autoencoders
landmarks.maturityNote: Used by labs for analysis and steering; tooling emerging.
landmarks.desc: Decomposing model activations into many sparse, interpretable features.

ref.title: Towards Monosemanticity: Decomposing Language Models With Dictionary Learning (Bricken et al.)

parents.why: Scalable method for finding interpretable features.

landmarks.name: Representation Engineering
landmarks.maturityNote: Moving from research into defensive prototypes.
landmarks.desc: Reading and steering high-level concepts in activation space to monitor or control behavior without retraining.

ref.title: Representation Engineering: A Top-Down Approach to AI Transparency (Zou et al.)

parents.why: Top-down use of internal representations for control.

landmarks.name: Circuit Breakers
landmarks.maturityNote: Research with limited deployment.
landmarks.desc: Training models so internal representations associated with harmful outputs are rerouted, interrupting generation.

ref.title: Improving Alignment and Robustness with Circuit Breakers (Zou et al.)

parents.why: Uses representation control as a safety mechanism.
Designed to resist adversarial attacks.

landmarks.name: Model and System Cards
landmarks.maturityNote: Expected for major releases and referenced in regulation.
landmarks.desc: Standardized documentation of a model's intended use, evaluations, limitations, and safety testing.

ref.title: Model Cards for Model Reporting (Mitchell et al.)

external.name: datasheets-and-documentation
external.why: Brings structured documentation practice to ML models.

landmarks.name: Human-AI Interaction Guidelines
landmarks.maturityNote: Widely cited baseline for AI product design.
landmarks.desc: Validated design guidelines for AI systems — set expectations, support correction, explain behavior, adapt over time.

ref.title: Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction (Amershi et al., CHI 2019)

parents.why: Codifies mixed-initiative principles into testable guidelines.

landmarks.name: Chat Interfaces
landmarks.maturityNote: The default AI product surface.
landmarks.desc: Turn-based conversational interfaces to general-purpose models, the dominant surface for AI products.

ref.title: Introducing ChatGPT (OpenAI, November 2022)

parents.why: Revives dialogue interfaces with general-purpose models.
Made practical by RLHF-tuned conversational models.

landmarks.name: Streaming Responses
landmarks.maturityNote: Universal pattern for text generation products.
landmarks.desc: Showing tokens as they are generated to cut perceived latency and let users interrupt early.

ref.title: OpenAI API streaming support

parents.why: Exposes token-by-token generation to the interface.

landmarks.name: Copilots and Inline Assistance
landmarks.maturityNote: Established pattern across editors and productivity tools.
landmarks.desc: AI suggestions embedded directly in a user's working context, accepted or rejected with low friction.

ref.title: Evaluating Large Language Models Trained on Code (Chen et al.)

parents.why: System takes initiative with suggestions; the user keeps control.
Code- and text-trained models power the suggestions.

landmarks.name: Citation and Grounding UX
landmarks.maturityNote: Expected in search and research products.
landmarks.desc: Linking claims in a response to the sources they came from so users can verify them.

ref.title: Perplexity AI launch (December 2022)

parents.why: Surfaces retrieved sources in the interface.
Implements 'make clear why the system did what it did'.

landmarks.name: Human-in-the-Loop Approval
landmarks.maturityNote: Essential for agents taking real actions.
landmarks.desc: Agents pause before consequential actions and ask the user to approve, edit, or reject them.

ref.title: LangGraph human-in-the-loop documentation

parents.why: Keeps the human as decision-maker at key points.
Approval gates tool calls before execution.

landmarks.name: Generative UI
landmarks.maturityNote: Adopted in products; patterns still forming.
landmarks.desc: Models emit structured payloads the front end renders as interactive components instead of plain text.

ref.title: Introducing AI SDK 3.0 with Generative UI support (Vercel, 2024)

parents.why: Structured output drives component rendering.
Returns manipulable interface elements instead of prose.

landmarks.name: Canvases and Artifacts
landmarks.maturityNote: Shipping in major assistants; conventions still settling.
landmarks.desc: A persistent, editable work object beside the conversation that the user and model revise together.

ref.title: Claude 3.5 Sonnet launch with Artifacts (Anthropic, June 2024)

parents.why: Users edit the work product directly.
Moves output out of the chat stream into a shared object.

landmarks.name: Contrastive Image-Text Pretraining
landmarks.maturityNote: Foundational component of vision-language systems.
landmarks.desc: Training image and text encoders so matching pairs land close together in a shared embedding space.

ref.title: Learning Transferable Visual Models From Natural Language Supervision (Radford et al.)

parents.why: Uses transformer encoders for both modalities.

landmarks.name: Vision-Language Models
landmarks.maturityNote: Standard capability of frontier APIs.
landmarks.desc: Language models that accept images (and often video) alongside text by projecting visual features into the model.

ref.title: Visual Instruction Tuning (Liu et al.)

parents.why: Uses pretrained vision encoders such as CLIP.
Connects visual features to an LLM.

landmarks.name: Document Understanding
landmarks.maturityNote: Rapidly replacing legacy OCR in RAG ingestion.
landmarks.desc: Extracting text, tables, and structure from documents with vision models rather than brittle OCR pipelines.

ref.title: OCR-free Document Understanding Transformer (Kim et al.)

parents.why: Reads page images end to end with transformers; VLMs now dominate this role.

landmarks.name: Visual Document Retrieval
landmarks.maturityNote: Promising; early production use.
landmarks.desc: Retrieving documents by embedding page images directly, skipping text extraction.

ref.title: ColPali: Efficient Document Retrieval with Vision Language Models (Faysse et al.)

parents.why: Uses VLM embeddings of page images.
Multi-vector dense retrieval over images.

landmarks.name: Speech Recognition
landmarks.maturityNote: Commodity capability.
landmarks.desc: Transcribing spoken audio to text with large weakly supervised transformer models.

ref.title: Robust Speech Recognition via Large-Scale Weak Supervision (Radford et al.)

parents.why: Encoder-decoder audio-to-text modeling.

landmarks.name: Realtime Voice Agents
landmarks.maturityNote: In production for support and assistants; latency and turn-taking still hard.
landmarks.desc: Low-latency spoken conversation with interruption handling, either end-to-end audio models or ASR-LLM-TTS pipelines.

ref.title: Hello GPT-4o (OpenAI, May 2024)

parents.why: Pipelines start from transcription; end-to-end models subsume it.
An LLM drives the conversation.

landmarks.name: Diffusion Models
landmarks.maturityNote: Dominant approach to media generation.
landmarks.desc: Generative models that learn to reverse a gradual noising process, now standard for images, audio, and video.

ref.title: Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (Ho et al.)

external.name: nonequilibrium-thermodynamics-generative-modeling
external.why: Builds on early diffusion probabilistic models (Sohl-Dickstein et al. 2015).

landmarks.name: Text-to-Image Generation
landmarks.maturityNote: Mature APIs and open models.
landmarks.desc: Generating images from text prompts, typically with latent diffusion guided by text encoders.

ref.title: High-Resolution Image Synthesis with Latent Diffusion Models (Rombach et al.)

parents.why: Runs diffusion in a compressed latent space with text conditioning.
Uses CLIP-style text encoders for conditioning.

landmarks.name: Video Generation
landmarks.maturityNote: Commercial APIs available; consistency and control still limited.
landmarks.desc: Generating video from text or images with diffusion transformers over spacetime patches.

ref.title: Video generation models as world simulators (OpenAI, February 2024)

parents.why: Extends image diffusion across time.
Uses diffusion transformers over spacetime patches.
